summary: Rabbi Meir says all the roofs of a city count as one area, so we may carry between them if they are about the same height. The Sages say each roof is its own area. Rabbi Shimon teaches about things that were already outside when Shabbos began.

chunks.en: All the roofs of the city
chunks.st: All the roofs of the city

chunks.en: are one area,
chunks.st: are considered one domain.
chunks.stMore: It is permitted to carry from one roof to another, even if the residents of the houses did not establish an eiruv between them. The Sages did not prohibit carrying between roofs, as it is rare to transfer an item from one roof to another.

chunks.en: as long as one roof is not ten tefachim higher
chunks.st: However, it is only permitted to transfer objects between roofs provided that one roof is neither ten handbreadths higher

chunks.en: or ten tefachim lower,
chunks.st: nor ten handbreadths lower than the adjacent roof.

chunks.en: says Rabbi Meir.
chunks.st: This is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

chunks.en: But the Sages say,
chunks.st: And the Rabbis say:

chunks.he: כָּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד רְשׁוּת בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ.
chunks.en: each and every one is an area by itself.
chunks.st: Each and every one of the roofs is a domain in and of itself.
chunks.stMore: It is permitted to carry from one to the other only if the residents of both houses established an eiruv.

chunks.en: Rabbi Shimon says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Shimon says:

chunks.he: אֶחָד גַּגּוֹת וְאֶחָד חֲצֵרוֹת וְאֶחָד קַרְפֵּיפוֹת,
chunks.en: roofs, courtyards, and storage yards together
chunks.st: Roofs, courtyards, and enclosures

chunks.en: are one area for things that were inside them when Shabbos began,
chunks.st: are all one domain with regard to vessels that were inside them when Shabbat began,
chunks.stMore: and one may therefore carry from one of these areas to another.

chunks.en: but not for things that were inside the house when Shabbos began.
chunks.st: However, they are not one domain with regard to vessels that were inside the house when Shabbat began and were later taken into one of the above domains. A vessel that was inside the house when Shabbat began and subsequently carried to one of these areas may be carried from one roof, courtyard, or enclosure to another only if an eiruv had been established between the domains.

summary: A big roof or courtyard next to a small one may be used, but the small one may not. A courtyard that broke open to the street is argued about: Rabbi Eliezer says it becomes like the street, the Sages say it is a karmelis.

chunks.en: A big roof next to a small one,
chunks.st: If a large roof was adjacent to a small roof,
chunks.stMore: and the boundary between them was no wider than ten cubits,

chunks.en: the big one is allowed and the small one is forbidden.
chunks.st: use of the large one is permitted, i.e., one may bring objects up to the roof from the house below and carry them on the roof, and use of the small one is prohibited.

chunks.en: A big courtyard that broke open into a small one,
chunks.st: A similar halakha applies to a large courtyard that was breached into a small one,
chunks.stMore: in a manner that one entire side of the small courtyard was breached, but the breach was less than ten cubits;

chunks.en: the big one is allowed,
chunks.st: it is permitted for the residents of the large courtyard to carry,

chunks.en: and the small one is forbidden,
chunks.st: but it is prohibited for the residents of the small one to do so.

chunks.en: because the gap is like a doorway of the big one.
chunks.explain: For the big one, walls are left on both sides of the gap.
chunks.st: The rationale for this difference is because in that case, the legal status of the breach is like that of the entrance of the large courtyard.
chunks.stMore: As the breach in the wall of the larger courtyard is surrounded on both sides by the remaining portions of that wall, and the breach is no greater than ten cubits wide, its legal status is like that of an entrance in the wall of the courtyard, and therefore it is permitted to carry in the large courtyard. With regard to the small courtyard, however, since one entire side of the small courtyard was breached, there remains no partition whatsoever on that side and carrying in that courtyard is therefore prohibited.

chunks.en: A courtyard that broke open to the public street,
chunks.st: With regard to a courtyard that was breached into the public domain,
chunks.stMore: and the breach was more than ten cubits wide, so that it cannot be considered an entrance,

chunks.en: someone who brings something from it into a private area,
chunks.st: one who carries an object from inside the courtyard into the private domain,

chunks.en: or from a private area into it,
chunks.st: or from the private domain into it,

chunks.en: is chayav, says Rabbi Eliezer.
chunks.explain: Chayav means he broke a Torah law of Shabbos.
chunks.st: is liable, as it ceases to be a private domain and is subsumed into the public domain. This is the statement of Rabbi Eliezer.

words.note: Guilty of breaking a Torah law.

chunks.en: But the Sages say,
chunks.st: And the Rabbis disagree and say:

chunks.en: from it into the public street,
chunks.st: One who carries from inside the courtyard into the public domain,

chunks.en: or from the public street into it,
chunks.st: or from the public domain into it,

chunks.en: he is patur, because it is like a karmelis.
chunks.explain: A karmelis is an in-between area, forbidden only by the Rabbis.
chunks.st: is exempt, because its legal status is like that of a karmelit. Although it ceases to be a private domain, it does not become a full-fledged public domain.

words.note: Not guilty of breaking a Torah law.
An area that is not fully private or public.

summary: If a courtyard or house broke open on Shabbos, or an alleyway's korah or lechi was taken away, Rabbi Yehudah says we may carry there for the rest of that Shabbos only. Rabbi Yosi disagrees.

chunks.he: חָצֵר שֶׁנִּפְרְצָה לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים מִשְּׁתֵּי רוּחוֹתֶיהָ,
chunks.en: A courtyard that broke open to the public street on two sides,
chunks.st: With regard to a courtyard that was breached on Shabbat into a public domain from two of its sides,

chunks.en: and also a house that broke open on two sides,
chunks.st: and likewise with regard to a house that was breached from two of its sides,

chunks.he: וְכֵן מָבוֹי שֶׁנִּטְּלוּ קוֹרוֹתָיו אוֹ לְחָיָיו,
chunks.en: and also an alleyway whose korah or lechi were taken away,
chunks.st: and likewise with regard to an alleyway whose cross beams or side posts were removed

chunks.he: מֻתָּרִין בְּאוֹתוֹ שַׁבָּת וַאֲסוּרִין לֶעָתִיד לָבֹא,
chunks.en: are allowed on that Shabbos and forbidden in the future,
chunks.st: the residents of that domain are permitted to carry there on that Shabbat, but are prohibited from doing so in the future.

chunks.en: says Rabbi Yehudah.
chunks.st: This is the statement of Rabbi Yehuda.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yosi says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Yosei says:
chunks.stMore: This cannot be the halakha, as

chunks.en: if they are allowed on that Shabbos,
chunks.st: if they are permitted to carry there on that Shabbat,

chunks.en: they are allowed in the future.
chunks.st: they are likewise permitted to do so in the future,

chunks.en: And if they are forbidden in the future,
chunks.st: and if they are prohibited from carrying there in the future,

chunks.en: they are forbidden on that Shabbos.
chunks.st: they are also prohibited from carrying there on that Shabbat.

summary: Rabbi Yehudah says we may carry under a room built across two houses or under a bridge, and that an alleyway open on both ends can have an eiruv. The Sages forbid both.

chunks.he: הַבּוֹנֶה עֲלִיָּה עַל גַּבֵּי שְׁנֵי בָתִּים,
chunks.en: Someone who builds an upstairs room on top of two houses,
chunks.st: With regard to one who builds an upper story atop two houses
chunks.stMore: on opposite sides of a public domain that passes beneath it,

chunks.en: and also bridges that are open on both ends,
chunks.st: and likewise bridges with a thoroughfare
chunks.stMore: beneath them that rest on walls on opposite sides of a public domain,

chunks.en: we may carry under them on Shabbos,
chunks.st: one may carry beneath the upper story and beneath the bridge on Shabbat.

chunks.en: says Rabbi Yehudah.
chunks.st: This is the statement of Rabbi Yehuda,
chunks.stMore: who maintains that these areas are considered private domains.

chunks.en: And the Sages forbid it.
chunks.st: And the Rabbis prohibit

chunks.en: And Rabbi Yehudah also said,
chunks.st: And furthermore, Rabbi Yehuda said:

chunks.en: we may make an eiruv for an alleyway open on both ends.
chunks.st: One may establish an eiruv even for an alleyway that is open
chunks.stMore: at both ends, with no need for any additional measures,

chunks.en: And the Sages forbid it.
chunks.st: and the Rabbis prohibit doing so.
